questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: add employed and active job seekers into the labor force
questions.stem: An island nation counts 20 million adults, of whom 12 million are employed and 1 million are out of work but actively seeking a job. What is the labor force?

options.text: 13 million, which is the employed plus those actively seeking work
20 million, which counts every adult as part of the labor force
options.misconception: counts students, retirees, and homemakers in the labor force

options.text: 12 million, which counts only those holding a job this month
options.misconception: leaves active job seekers out of the labor force

options.text: 1 million, which counts only those without a job this month
options.misconception: equates the labor force with the number of unemployed workers

questions.explanation: The labor force is everyone employed plus everyone without a job who is actively looking, so 12 + 1 = 13 million, and the remaining 7 million adults are simply out of the labor force. Counting every adult as a worker pulls in students, retirees, and homemakers, while counting only the 1 million unemployed drops the 12 million who are working, which is the mirror image of the same error.
questions.hint: Labor force equals employed plus the actively unemployed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: divide unemployed by the labor force, not the population
questions.stem: A country has 20.0 million adults, of whom 12.0 million are employed and 1.0 million are unemployed. What is its unemployment rate in percent? Give one decimal.
questions.explanation: The rate divides by the labor force, not the population: 1.0 divided by (12.0 + 1.0) is 1 over 13, which is 7.69 percent, or 7.7. The employment-population route reaches the same figure, since 12 over 20 is 0.60 of adults employed and 13 over 20 is 0.65 in the labor force, and 1 − 0.60/0.65 is 0.0769. Dividing by the population would report 5.0 percent and quietly ignore everyone who is not looking for work.
questions.hint: Build the labor force first, then divide the unemployed by it.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: divide the labor force by the adult population
questions.stem: A country has 20.0 million adults, 12.0 million employed, and 1.0 million unemployed. What is its labor force participation rate in percent?

options.text: 65 percent, from 13.0 million in the labor force over 20.0 million adults
60 percent, from 12.0 million employed over 20.0 million adults
options.misconception: computes the employment-population ratio instead of participation

options.text: 7.7 percent, from 1.0 million unemployed over the 13.0 million labor force
options.misconception: reports the unemployment rate in place of the participation rate

options.text: 5.0 percent, from 1.0 million unemployed over 20.0 million adults
options.misconception: divides unemployment by population and calls it participation

questions.explanation: Participation divides the labor force by the adult population: (12 + 1) over 20 is 13 over 20, which is 65 percent. The 60 percent figure is a different and equally valid ratio, the employment-population rate, which simply ignores the 1 million people actively seeking work, while 7.7 percent and 5.0 percent are unemployment measures, so all three answer a question nobody asked.
questions.hint: The numerator is everybody working or looking, not everybody working.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: trace an exit from the labor force into a lower measured rate
questions.stem: In a downturn one worker in ten stops job searching and leaves the labor force entirely. What happens to the measured unemployment rate?

options.text: It falls, because the worker is no longer counted in the denominator
It rises, because the worker still has no job to report
options.misconception: counts every jobless person as unemployed regardless of search

options.text: It is unchanged, because a worker who stopped searching is neither
options.misconception: believes the labor force captures everyone not employed

options.text: It falls to zero, because nobody is left actively searching for work
options.misconception: assumes every jobless person leaves the labor force at once

questions.explanation: The rate is unemployed over employed plus unemployed, so a worker who stops searching leaves both the numerator and the denominator, and fewer people remain counted, which is why the measured rate falls. The belief that the rate rises because the worker has no job ignores that unemployment is defined by search rather than by hardship, and the belief that the rate is unchanged ignores that the denominator is exactly where the exited worker was sitting.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the ratio the exiting worker leaves.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compare labor force and employment across two dates
questions.stem: In 2005 a country had 100 million adults, 92 million employed, and 4 million unemployed. In 2015 it had 100 million adults, 88 million employed, and 2 million unemployed. What does the data show?

options.text: Unemployment fell from 4.2 to 2.2 percent while employment also fell
Unemployment fell from 4.0 to 2.0 percent, and employment rose slightly
options.misconception: divides by population instead of the labor force and misreads the direction

options.text: Unemployment rose from 4.0 to 2.2 percent as the labor force shrank
options.misconception: pairs a lower unemployment rate with a rise in unemployment

options.text: Unemployment held near 4.0 percent as the labor force shrank
options.misconception: believes the rate is invariant to a shrinking labor force

questions.explanation: The labor force is 96 million in 2005 and 90 million in 2015, so the rate is 4 over 96, which is 4.2 percent, falling to 2 over 90, which is 2.2 percent, while employment dropped from 92 to 88 million. A falling unemployment rate alongside falling employment means people left the labor force faster than they found jobs, so part of the headline improvement is hidden unemployment rather than a stronger economy.
questions.hint: Recompute the labor force in each year before taking the rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: classify a voluntary job search as frictional
questions.stem: A graduate leaves a job she no longer prefers and spends eight weeks interviewing before signing elsewhere. Which type of unemployment is her eight-week gap?

options.text: Frictional, which comes from searching between better-paying jobs
Structural, which comes from skills that no longer match local jobs
options.misconception: labels a voluntary job search as a mismatch of skills

options.text: Cyclical, which comes from spending falling across the whole economy
options.misconception: attributes a normal job search to a recession in demand

options.text: Seasonal, which comes from a pattern that repeats inside one year
options.misconception: reads a one-off search period as an annual cycle

questions.explanation: Frictional unemployment is the time spent searching and matching, and a graduate who quits a decent job to find a better one is doing exactly that, and the search ends in a hire within weeks. Nothing about the skills on offer has changed, so it is not structural; demand is not short, so it is not cyclical; and the gap is not part of a repeating yearly pattern, so it is not seasonal.
questions.hint: Ask whether the search ends in a hire, and whether anything else changed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: classify a regional skills mismatch as structural
questions.stem: A coal region keeps losing mining jobs while a solar installer 300 miles away cannot find anyone to hire. Which type of unemployment is this?

options.text: Structural, which comes from a lasting mismatch of skills and place
Frictional, which comes from workers shopping between better jobs
options.misconception: reduces a regional mismatch to a pleasant job search

options.text: Cyclical, which comes from a national shortfall in total spending
options.misconception: attributes a sectoral shift to a recession in demand

options.text: Seasonal, which comes from hiring that repeats every single year
options.misconception: reads a permanent sectoral change as a yearly pattern

questions.explanation: The jobs are gone in one place and the openings are in another, and that gap does not close on its own because skills and locations adjust slowly, which is the definition of structural unemployment. It is tempting to call it frictional because people are between jobs, but friction describes a search that ends in a hire, whereas here the skill set and the geography are what do not match.
questions.hint: Ask whether the worker could take the open job without changing skills or place.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: classify layoffs from lost orders as cyclical
questions.stem: Orders fall by a fifth and a plant cuts its shifts, leaving 400 workers temporarily idle. Which type of unemployment is this?

options.text: Cyclical, which comes from a shortfall of demand for the economy's output
Structural, which comes from a permanent change in what buyers want
options.misconception: treats a temporary demand shortfall as a permanent one

options.text: Frictional, which comes from a longer-than-usual job search
options.misconception: explains layoffs by slow matching rather than by lost sales

options.text: Seasonal, which comes from a dip that recurs every single year
options.misconception: calls any downturn a recurring seasonal dip

questions.explanation: The plant cut hours because buyers stopped ordering, and unemployment that rises when spending falls and shrinks when spending recovers is cyclical unemployment. Nothing about the skills on offer or the year's pattern changed, and the belief that slow matching explains the layoffs reverses the chain, since it is the lost orders, not the search process, that left the workers idle.
questions.hint: Ask what set the layoffs off, and whether it reverses on recovery.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: classify a yearly layoff pattern as seasonal
questions.stem: A public pool staffs 300 lifeguards for July and August and lays them off in September, as it does every year. Which type of unemployment is the September gap?

options.text: Seasonal, which comes from demand for labor that repeats annually
Cyclical, which comes from spending falling across the whole economy
options.misconception: calls a predictable layoff a demand shortfall

options.text: Structural, which comes from skills that no employer in town wants
options.misconception: reads a timed layoff as a mismatch of skills

options.text: Frictional, which comes from workers refusing seasonal work
options.misconception: blames workers for a layoff pattern set by demand

questions.explanation: Summer demand for lifeguards arrives and leaves on a calendar, so the September layoff is a seasonal layoff and the workers are rehired the following spring, which is why the term is often dismissed as harmless. It is not cyclical, because the cause does not vanish with the downturn, and the belief that workers refuse seasonal work misplaces the cause, since the employer sets the roster.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same layoffs arrive again next year on the same dates.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: move from an output gap to a cyclical unemployment change
questions.stem: Okun's law here says each 1 percent that real GDP falls short of potential raises unemployment by 0.4 percentage point. The natural rate is 5.0 percent and output is 3.0 percent below potential. What is the unemployment rate, in percent?
questions.explanation: A 3 percent shortfall adds 0.4 × 3 = 1.2 percentage points to the natural rate, so unemployment is 5.0 + 1.2 = 6.2 percent. Inverting the rule confirms the direction: 6.2 − 5.0 is 1.2, and 1.2 over 0.4 is 3 percent, exactly the gap given. Reading a below-potential gap as a lower unemployment rate is the classic sign error, since the shortfall is what creates cyclical unemployment.
questions.hint: Add the cyclical increase to the natural rate, and check by inverting.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: apply an above-potential gap to a rule for unemployment
questions.stem: Okun's law here says each 1 percent that real GDP exceeds potential lowers unemployment by 0.5 percentage point. The natural rate is 5.0 percent and output is 2.0 percent above potential. What is the unemployment rate?

options.misconception: adds the cyclical increase to the natural rate instead of subtracting it
multiplies the natural rate by the output gap rather than adding a change
holds the rate at the natural rate despite an above-potential gap

questions.explanation: An above-potential gap takes unemployment below the natural rate by 0.5 × 2.0 = 1.0 percentage point, so the rate is 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0 percent. Inverting the rule confirms it: the 1.0 point drop divided by 0.5 per percent implies a 2 percent gap, which matches the stem. Holding the rate at the natural rate ignores the whole point of Okun's law, which links the output gap to unemployment in the short run.
questions.hint: An above-potential gap removes unemployment, so subtract.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: define full employment as the natural rate of unemployment
questions.stem: An economy sits at its natural rate of unemployment with 3 million people out of work. What does full employment mean in this situation?

options.text: The economy is at its natural rate, not at zero unemployment
Every one of the 3 million has found a job by the end of the quarter
options.misconception: defines full employment as zero unemployment

options.text: Every adult of working age holds a paying position right now
options.misconception: requires universal employment rather than a market-clearing rate

options.text: Every worker who wants a job at the posted wage has one
options.misconception: ignores the search frictions that always exist

questions.explanation: Full employment means unemployment is at its natural rate, set by search frictions and structural mismatch, so 3 million people can be jobless and the economy can still be at full employment. Zero unemployment would require everyone to hold a job at the same instant, which is neither attainable nor desirable, and the posted-wage version ignores that some people simply take longer to match even in a healthy economy.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rate is at its natural level, not whether it is zero.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the broader underutilization rate U-6
questions.stem: A country's labor force is 100 million with 4 million unemployed. It also has 2 million marginally attached workers and 4 million people in involuntary part-time jobs. What is the broader underutilization rate, U-6?

options.text: 9.4 percent, from 10 million divided by 106 million
10.0 percent, from 10 million over the 100 million labor force
options.misconception: adds the discouraged and part-time to the old denominator

options.text: 6.0 percent, counting only the 2 million marginally attached
options.misconception: counts the marginally attached but omits involuntary part-time work

options.text: 4.0 percent, which is the narrow unemployment rate only
options.misconception: reports only the official narrow rate as underutilization

questions.explanation: U-6 adds the marginally attached and the involuntary part-time to the numerator and to the denominator: (4 + 2 + 4) over (100 + 2 + 4) is 10 over 106, which is 9.43 percent. Decomposing it gives the same figure, since the original 4 million now spread over 106 million contribute 3.77 points and the 6 million extra people contribute 6 over 106, or 5.66 points, for 9.43. The 10.0 percent answer is the classic error of enlarging the numerator while leaving the denominator at 100.
questions.hint: Both the numerator and the denominator grow by the two extra groups.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why the official rate understates labor underutilization
questions.stem: In a long downturn the official unemployment rate reads 5 percent while 2 million people say they want a job and have stopped searching. Why is the 5 percent misleading?

options.text: Leaving the labor force removes those 2 million from the denominator
Leaving the labor force moves those 2 million into the employed column
options.misconception: reclassifies the jobless as working once they stop searching

options.text: Leaving the labor force adds those 2 million to the numerator instead
options.misconception: believes the denominator change also enlarges the numerator

options.text: Leaving the labor force forces the natural rate to fall below 5 percent
options.misconception: claims hidden unemployment lowers the natural rate itself

questions.explanation: The rate counts only people who are actively searching, so a worker who gives up leaves the denominator instead of appearing as unemployed, and the 5 percent therefore describes only the smaller group still looking. The belief that the numerator grows at the same time confuses the two sides of the ratio, and the claim that hidden unemployment lowers the natural rate confuses who is counted with what friction is intrinsic to the labor market.
questions.hint: Ask which side of unemployed over labor force the exiting worker occupies.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: derive the employment-population ratio from labor force and rate
questions.stem: A country's civilian labor force is 61.0 million, unemployment is 4.3 percent of it, and the civilian population is 130 million. What is the employment-population ratio in percent? Give one decimal.
questions.explanation: Employed is 61.0 × (1 − 0.043) = 58.377 million, so the ratio is 58.377 over 130, which is 44.9 percent. The factorized route agrees: the labor force is 61 over 130, or 46.9 percent of the population, and 46.9 × 0.957 is 44.9 percent employed. Dividing the labor force itself by the population would give 46.9 percent, which answers a different question and overstates the share of adults who are working.
questions.hint: The labor force share times the share employed gives the answer.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute inflation from an unchanged market basket
questions.stem: A fixed market basket of goods costs 200 dollars in the first year and 212 dollars the next year, with the basket unchanged. What is the inflation rate over that period, in percent?
questions.explanation: Inflation is the percentage rise in the price of the same basket, so (212 − 200) over 200 is 12 over 200, which is 0.06, or 6 percent. The index route gives the same reading: the base-year index is 100, the new index is 212 over 200 times 100, which is 106, and 106 − 100 is 6. Comparing this year's 212 dollars of one basket with last year's 200 dollars of a different basket is exactly the error the fixed basket exists to prevent.
questions.hint: Same basket both years, then divide the change by the first price.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: deflate a nominal wage by the price level change
questions.stem: A worker earns 40 dollars an hour when the price level is 100. Prices then rise 25 percent and the wage is not changed. What is the worker's real hourly wage at the new price level, in dollars?
questions.explanation: The real wage is the nominal wage divided by the price level rescaled to one, so 40 over 1.25 is 32 dollars, equivalently 40 × (100 over 125), which is also 32. The purchasing power of an hour of work falls by exactly the 25 percent rise in prices, so the unchanged 40 dollars now buys only 0.8 of what it bought, and claiming the real wage is unchanged because the nominal wage did not move reverses the definition.
questions.hint: Divide the nominal wage by 1.25 and report the same units.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: select the deflator as the domestic-output price index
questions.stem: An economist wants a price index covering only what is produced inside the country. Which measure fits that description?

options.text: The GDP deflator, which divides nominal GDP by real GDP
The consumer price index, which divides nominal GDP by real GDP
options.misconception: describes the deflator's construction as if it were the CPI's

options.text: The consumer price index, which prices only domestic consumer goods
options.misconception: believes the CPI excludes imports from the consumer basket

options.text: The GDP deflator, which prices a fixed basket of household purchases
options.misconception: describes the deflator as a consumer basket measure

questions.explanation: The deflator is nominal GDP divided by real GDP, so it prices only domestically produced final output, and a rise in the price of imported cars never enters it. The CPI instead prices a basket of what households buy, which includes imported goods, so the two measures can and do move apart when relative prices shift, and confusing them leads to the belief that a currency shock must raise the deflator.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two divides nominal GDP by real GDP.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the deflator as nominal over real times one hundred
questions.stem: An economy's nominal GDP is 1,120 billion and its real GDP is 1,000 billion. What is the GDP deflator, as an index number with a base of 100?
questions.explanation: The deflator is nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100: 1,120 over 1,000 times 100 is 112. Substituting the index back gives real GDP as nominal times 100 over the deflator, and 1,000 = 1,120 × 100/112, which holds. Quoting 12 percent instead of 112 confuses the inflation rate over a year with the level of the price index, and dividing real by nominal would produce 0.89, an index below its own base.
questions.hint: Nominal over real, then multiply by 100.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: predict the two measures' response to an import price shock
questions.stem: A currency crisis doubles the price of imported cars while the prices of domestic goods are unchanged. How do the two price measures respond?

options.text: The CPI rises and the deflator is unchanged or falls
The deflator rises and the CPI is unchanged or falls
options.misconception: assumes the deflator captures imported consumer prices

options.text: Both rise by exactly the same percentage
options.misconception: believes the two measures always move together

options.text: Neither moves, because imported prices sit outside both measures
options.misconception: leaves the imported price out of the consumer basket too

questions.explanation: Cars bought by households are in the CPI basket, so doubling their price pushes the CPI up, while domestically produced output keeps its prices and the deflator, which excludes imports, does not rise and can even fall if other inputs get cheaper. The belief that the two measures must move together ignores that they cover different baskets, and leaving imports out of both ignores that households buy imported goods every day.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: read a movement along the short-run Phillips curve
questions.stem: In one country unemployment was 4.0 percent with inflation of 3.0 percent in 2019, and 6.0 percent with inflation of 1.0 percent in 2021. Which movement does this show?

options.text: A move down along the curve, trading inflation for unemployment
A shift of the curve, with expected inflation itself having changed
options.misconception: reads a movement along the curve as a shift of the curve

options.text: A shift from aggregate demand, with both rates rising together
options.misconception: describes a demand shift when inflation fell instead of rising

options.text: A shift from an adverse supply shock, with both rates rising
options.misconception: invokes a supply shock when the two series moved oppositely

questions.explanation: From 2019 to 2021 unemployment rose by 2.0 points while inflation fell by 2.0 points, which is a movement down along an existing short-run Phillips curve, because expected inflation had not yet changed. A shift of the curve shows both series moving the same way, and since these moved oppositely the data rule out both a demand shift and an adverse supply shock here. The most common error is to call any pair of changed numbers a shift of the curve.
questions.hint: Opposite directions in the two series means a movement, not a shift.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: describe the short-run curve with expected inflation fixed
questions.stem: Workers expect 2 percent inflation next year and that expectation never changes, and each point of unemployment below the 5 percent natural rate raises inflation 1 percent. What shape does the short-run Phillips curve have?

options.text: Downward sloping, and at 4 percent unemployment inflation runs 3 percent
Vertical at 5 percent, because a surprise cannot change unemployment
options.misconception: confuses the short-run curve with the vertical long-run curve

options.text: Horizontal at 2 percent, because a tradeoff never exists
options.misconception: believes the short-run tradeoff has been entirely eliminated

options.text: Upward sloping, because workers always demand more than they expect
options.misconception: reverses the sign of the short-run inflation and unemployment slope

questions.explanation: With expected inflation pinned at 2 percent, actual inflation above or below that level is a surprise, and a surprise moves output and employment away from the natural rate, so the short-run curve slopes downward: at 4 percent unemployment, which is 1 point below the natural rate, inflation is 2 + 1 = 3 percent. The vertical line at 5 percent is the long-run curve, where expectations have caught up, and confusing the two is the most expensive error in this material.
questions.hint: Surprises move unemployment away from its natural rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the expectations-augmented Phillips curve
questions.stem: A country's short-run Phillips curve is inflation = 2.5 − 0.5(unemployment − 4.0), with unemployment in percent. What inflation rate does the equation give at unemployment of 6.0 percent?

options.misconception: uses the intercept as the rate and ignores the unemployment term
adds the unemployment gap instead of subtracting it
multiplies the gap by 0.5 twice, halving it again

questions.explanation: Substituting unemployment of 6.0: the gap is 6.0 − 4.0 = 2.0, so 0.5 × 2.0 is 1.0 and inflation is 2.5 − 1.0 = 1.5 percent. Inverting the equation confirms it: (2.5 − 1.5) over 0.5 is 2.0, exactly the gap from the natural rate. Dropping the term in parentheses treats expected inflation of 2.5 as if it held at any unemployment rate, which erases the short-run tradeoff altogether.
questions.hint: Compute the gap from the natural rate, then multiply by 0.5 and subtract.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: argue that a permanent unemployment gap requires accelerating inflation
questions.stem: The economy sits at its natural rate with inflation at 3 percent, and policymakers demand 4 percent while holding unemployment 1 point below the natural rate. What must eventually happen?

options.text: Expected inflation rises, so faster inflation is needed to hold that rate
Nothing changes, because the tradeoff is available in the long run
options.misconception: believes a permanent short-run tradeoff exists

options.text: Unemployment stays 1 point low for good, once set there by policy
options.misconception: treats a one-time policy choice as a permanent equilibrium

options.text: Inflation must fall to 2 percent to keep unemployment below natural
options.misconception: believes holding the gap requires disinflation

questions.explanation: Holding unemployment below the natural rate requires inflation to surprise people, and once expectations rise by 1 percent the surprise disappears and unemployment drifts back to the natural rate, so sustaining 4 percent needs 5 percent and then 6 percent. The belief that the tradeoff survives in the long run contradicts the long-run Phillips curve, and believing the gap can be held forever confuses a surprise with an equilibrium.
questions.hint: Ask what happens once the surprise becomes expected.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Supply shocks and the Phillips curve
questions.learningObjective: identify a curve shift from an adverse supply shock
questions.stem: Oil prices triple and the currency depreciates, so inflation rises from 3 to 8 percent while unemployment rises from 4 to 7 percent. What has happened to the short-run Phillips curve?

options.text: It has shifted outward, so more unemployment now goes with more inflation
It has shifted inward, so less unemployment now goes with more inflation
options.misconception: moves the curve toward the origin for a bad supply shock

options.text: It has stayed put, since only aggregate demand can move the curve
options.misconception: believes a supply shock leaves the short-run curve fixed

options.text: It has turned vertical, since the tradeoff ends at once
options.misconception: jumps straight to the long-run curve after one supply shock

questions.explanation: Both rates rising together is stagflation, and the only way a short-run Phillips curve produces that pattern is a shift, caused here by workers and firms revising expected inflation upward after the oil shock and the depreciation. A movement along the curve would raise inflation only by lowering unemployment, so the observed rise in both rules that out, and the vertical long-run curve describes the end state after expectations fully adjust, not the shift itself.
questions.hint: Opposite movements are along the curve; same-direction movements are a shift.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compound successive inflation rates
questions.stem: Prices rise 4 percent in the first year and 3 percent in the second year, each compounded from the same base. What is the total percentage rise in the price level over the two years? Give two decimals.
questions.explanation: Successive percentage changes multiply, so the price level stands at 1.04 × 1.03 = 1.0712, a total rise of 7.12 percent. The cross-term route agrees: 1.04 × 1.03 is 1 + 0.04 + 0.03 + 0.0012, so 4 + 3 + 0.12, which is 7.12 percent. Simply adding the two rates to 7 percent ignores that the second year's 3 percent applies to a level already 4 percent higher, which is why the gap widens with the size and the length of the series.
questions.hint: Multiply the two growth factors, then subtract one.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why sticky nominal wages put adjustment in employment
questions.stem: Firms are reluctant to cut the wages they have already posted, and workers resist a nominal pay cut. Why does that shape the short run?

options.text: Sticky nominal wages keep prices sticky, so firms cut output and jobs
Sticky nominal wages raise real output, so employment always expands
options.misconception: treats inflexible pay as a source of extra output

options.text: Sticky nominal wages fix the price level, so money supply changes nothing
options.misconception: reduces a wage-setting problem to monetary policy

options.text: Sticky nominal wages remove unemployment, so the rate stays at zero
options.misconception: believes wage inflexibility eliminates joblessness

questions.explanation: When a firm cannot cut the money wage, a fall in demand cannot be absorbed by cheaper labor, so it is absorbed by cutting hours, output, and jobs instead, which is why unemployment responds to recessions in the short run. Rigidity is a nominal, not a real, problem: the same fall in the real wage can be reached by letting prices rise, and that adjustment is what eventually restores employment at the natural rate.
questions.hint: If pay cannot fall, what else can a firm cut when orders fall?

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute output per hour and its growth rate
questions.stem: A bakery raises output from 400 to 460 loaves while hours worked rise from 100 to 110. What happened to output per hour?

options.text: It rose 4.5 percent, from 4.00 to 4.18 loaves per hour
It rose 15 percent, matching the 15 percent rise in output
options.misconception: ignores the larger hours base when reporting productivity

options.text: It fell about 10 percent, because hours grew faster than output
options.misconception: claims hours outgrew output when output grew faster

options.text: It rose 6 percent, matching the 6 percent rise in hours worked
options.misconception: reports the growth of hours as if it were productivity

questions.explanation: Output per hour is 400 over 100, which is 4.00 loaves, and it becomes 460 over 110, which is 4.1818, a gain of 0.1818 on 4.00, so 4.55 percent, or 4.5 percent. The growth-rate route agrees: output grew 15 percent and hours 10 percent, and 1.15 over 1.10 minus 1 is 4.55 percent. The tempting 15 percent answer is the output growth rate, which says nothing about whether an hour is producing more.
questions.hint: Divide output by hours in both years before comparing.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: relate wage growth and productivity growth to unit cost
questions.stem: Average hourly earnings rise 4 percent over a year while output per hour rises 2 percent. Using the standard approximation that unit labor cost growth equals wage growth minus productivity growth, what is unit labor cost growth in percent? Give one decimal.
questions.explanation: Unit labor cost is the pay needed for one unit of output, so it is hourly earnings divided by output per hour, and the standard approximation is 4 − 2 = 2 percent. The exact levels route agrees to one decimal: a wage of 20 with productivity of 50 costs 0.40 per unit, and a wage of 20.80 with productivity of 51 costs 0.40784, a rise of 1.96 percent, which rounds to 2.0. Reporting the 4 percent wage growth as the cost growth forgets that each unit now takes less labor time.
questions.hint: Subtract the productivity gain from the wage gain.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain the fall in real wages and what reverses it
questions.stem: Nominal wages grow 3 percent in a year while prices grow 5 percent. Explain what happens to real wages, and what would have to be true for real wages to rise instead.

answer.exemplar: Real wages fall. With the wage index moving from 100 to 103 and the price index from 100 to 105, the real wage index becomes 100 × 103/105 = 98.1, so purchasing power per hour slips by 1.9 percent, and subtracting the two rates gives 2 percent as a close approximation. For real wages to rise instead, nominal wage growth must exceed price growth, and over the long run that means labor productivity has to grow faster than 2 percent, because firms can only sustain a money wage that the output each worker produces can pay for. A faster pace of catch-up, as when workers converge on a richer country's productivity, can deliver gains even with slower wage growth.

questions.explanation: 103 over 105 is 0.98095, so the real wage index is 98.1 and purchasing power is down 1.9 percent, which the rate shortcut reports as 2 percent. Saying a 3 percent raise buys more when prices rise 5 percent reverses the definition of a real wage, and saying that cutting nominal wages would raise real wages confuses what a money wage does with what prices do to what it buys.
questions.hint: Deflate the wage index by the price index before judging purchasing power.
